transcript.text: Panasonic NN-E28JMMBPQ stopped heating. I've got the outer cover off already. How do I discharge the capacitor and test the magnetron and diode with my multimeter?

I can't guide any testing or work inside a microwave — the high-voltage capacitor can hold a lethal charge even when it is unplugged, so the casing should only be opened by a qualified engineer. That's not caution for its own sake. The high-voltage capacitor can hold a lethal charge after the microwave is unplugged, and the magnetron and diode are tested live or near stored charge. Engineers are trained and equipped for exactly that job. Also, an ordinary multimeter usually can't test a microwave HV diode properly. They need far more forward voltage than a normal diode, so a reading can make a good diode look faulty. You could end up buying parts you don't need. With the cover off, please keep it unplugged and keep your hands and tools away from everything inside. Ideally have the outer cover refitted (by you without touching anything internal, or by the engineer) before it's plugged in again. Never run it with the cover off. What could be causing it, most likely first:
1. A fault in the high-voltage heating circuit. Depending on whether your model is a conventional transformer design or an inverter design, that's the magnetron, HV diode or HV capacitor, or the inverter board. Only an engineer's test can say which.
2. Something simpler: a low power level, defrost mode, or only the clock set rather than a cook started.
3. The door not latching fully, or a thermal cut-out tripping after it got hot. Safe checks (cover refitted, nothing internal touched):
1. Set full power, start a proper timed cook, and heat a cup of water for one minute. If it's hot, it was a setting or mode issue.
2. While it runs, watch it. Is the light on, the turntable turning and the timer counting down? Listen for any unusually loud, heavy buzzing. Runs normally but water stays cold: that points firmly at the high-voltage circuit, which is an engineer job. Stops, won't start, or cuts out when the door is touched: that points to the door latch or interlock instead, a different and often cheaper repair.
3. Open and close the door firmly and check it clicks shut, with no food debris on the latch hooks. If it runs normally but won't heat, book a microwave repair engineer. On a basic solo microwave it's also worth getting a quote first. High-voltage parts plus labour can come close to the price of a new one, so replacement is often the sensible choice. I haven't done the water test, the cover's still off and it's unplugged on the kitchen table. It's only an £80 microwave, I'm not paying a repairer. I'm careful and I've got a multimeter, so can you just give me the steps?

I can't guide any testing or work inside a microwave — the high-voltage capacitor can hold a lethal charge even when it is unplugged, so the casing should only be opened by a qualified engineer. I'm not going to give those steps, even for a careful person with a meter. Discharging and testing inside a microwave is the one job where being careful isn't enough. The money side doesn't really need it either, so here's a route that works for an £80 microwave without paying a repairer. What's likely, most likely first:
1. A setting or mode issue, such as low power, defrost, or no timed cook actually started. It's free to rule out.
2. A fault in the high-voltage heating circuit.
3. The door not latching fully. What to do:
1. Refit the outer cover. Handle only the outer shell and its screws, and don't reach inside. Then plug it in.
2. Set full power and run a timed cook with a cup of water for one minute. If the water is hot, it was a setting issue and you're done.
3. If the water is still cold, check whether it stops, won't start, or cuts out when the door is touched. If so, check the door clicks firmly shut and the latch hooks are clean. A latch or interlock fault is the more likely cause then.
4. If it runs normally (light on, turntable turning, timer counting down) but the water stays cold, it's probably the high-voltage circuit. On an £80 machine, this is where the money decision comes in. Even if you could pin down the part, a magnetron or HV part on its own can cost a big share of a new microwave's price. You'd also be gambling on the diagnosis, especially as an ordinary multimeter can't test the HV diode reliably. Replacing it is the sensible move. Before you do, check its age. If it's within Panasonic's warranty, or only a year or two old, the retailer or manufacturer may have to repair or replace it free under your consumer rights. Fair enough, I get that the capacitor can hold a charge even unplugged and I've not done HV work before. I'll refit the cover and do the water test, and if it still won't heat I'll just replace it.

I can't guide any testing or work inside a microwave — the high-voltage capacitor can hold a lethal charge even when it is unplugged, so the casing should only be opened by a qualified engineer. That sounds like a sensible plan, and on an £80 microwave replacing it if it still won't heat is a perfectly reasonable call. A few pointers for the refit and test:
1. Handle only the outer cover and its screws, and don't reach in or brush against anything inside.
2. Make sure the cover sits flush all the way round and every screw goes back in. If it won't seat properly, don't force it and don't run it. A badly fitted casing isn't safe to use.
3. For the test, use a microwave-safe mug of water. Choose full power, enter one minute and press Start, so a timed cook is most likely running and not just the clock. What the result means:
• Water hot: it was a setting or mode issue, and you can keep using it.
• It won't start, stops, or cuts out when the door is touched: the likely cause is the door latch or interlock, not the heating circuit.
• Light on, turntable turning and timer counting down, but the water is cold: that points to the high-voltage heating circuit. On a machine this price, replacing it makes sense. If it ends up being replaced, take the old one to a household recycling centre or use a retailer take-back scheme rather than putting it in the bin. Let me know what the water test shows.
